title: His arranging style: counterpoint, offbeat voicings and chord colors
summary: Randolph describes writing in counterpoint rather than concerted style and finding his ahead-of-time harmonies hard to put over.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Inge was an arranger and I was an arranger.
I see. By this time you were writing arrangements?

Oh, yes, I was arranging then. I was using (unintelligible) characteristic of chords and rhythms that they are really doing (now) I was doing it back then in those times. Because everybody will tell me, you were ahead, and they couldn't -- and I had a hard time getting it through -- getting my work over, because of a little ahead of he had a time and they couldn't understand it.
In what way do you mean -- rhythmically?
Rhythmically was one way. The chords the characteristic of chords, they like the way it sound but they couldn't understand it. Then I wrote more like -- counter-

point. For instance, you're playing, but you -- you're playing with me in the section, but maybe you wouldn't be playing just the same thng that the other fellow's playing, you see. I wrote more in a counterpoint way.

Voicing, that's right. See, most of the bands wrote more concerted, you know, concerted way -- concerted like -- da-da-da-da -- well, if I would say da-da-da- see, I've got them mixed up in there. Then, I would have maybe the saxophones trilling -- this is very beautiful. The saxophone would be trilling on a certain chord -- while they're trilling on a certain chord, then I pick a tone out for their chord that's very brilliant and put the trumpets on there and let them give you somewhat of an offbeat. da-da-da-da Then I throw the rhythm against that ba -ba-ba-ba -- Then I would let my trombones come up ba-ba-ba-ba -- and all that mix. Well, when the trumpets get so high, then I would let them hit together and spread -- da-da-da-da-da--
I had a lot of fun.
